docs.explain:
UPPER makes every letter a capital, LOWER takes them all down, and PROPER capitalises the first letter of each word. Each takes one piece of text and returns new text. Digits, hyphens and spaces pass through untouched, and none of the three removes a space or fixes a spelling.

The first screen asks for ab-2291-xk as a shipping label, which is AB-2291-XK. UPPER is the only one of the three that gives that. PROPER returns Ab-2291-Xk, because it starts a new word after every hyphen.

The second screen has ada LOVELACE, and PROPER returns Ada Lovelace. The change runs one way: once UPPER has run, the original case is gone. Keep the source column when the spelling may matter later.

errors.text: The converted text was used in arithmetic, as in =UPPER(A2)/0.
UPPER was typed with an extra letter, which is a function the sheet has never heard of.
PROPER on a code starts a new word after each hyphen, so the label comes out Ab-2291-Xk.

seo.title: UPPER, LOWER and PROPER in Excel
seo.description: Three functions change case and nothing else. PROPER starts a new word after any punctuation, which is why the shipping label needs UPPER instead.
